title: How to Forget a Guy: 12 Steps to Finally Move On
h1: How to Forget a Guy: 12 Honest Steps to Finally Move On
description: Learn how to forget a guy you can't stop thinking about, whether he was an ex, a situationship or a crush, with 12 practical steps to heal and move on.
excerpt: Whether he was your ex, a situationship or a crush who never chose you, these 12 steps help you stop replaying him and get your life back.
intro:
He might have been your boyfriend of three years, a situationship that never got a label or a crush who just did not feel the same way. Either way, he is living rent-free in your head, and you are tired of it. You check his profile, replay old conversations and feel a jolt every time your phone buzzes.

Forgetting a guy is not about erasing him from your memory. It is about turning down the volume until he is just a person you used to know, not the center of your day. These 12 steps will help you create distance, process what happened and rebuild a life that feels exciting again.
body:
Start with why you need to let him go

Getting clear on your reason makes every other step easier, especially on the nights when you are tempted to text him. Maybe he cheated, maybe he did not want the same future, maybe he never committed, or maybe he is simply unavailable. Write your reason in one sentence and keep it in your phone notes. When nostalgia hits, read it.

Knowing the reason also helps you choose the right approach. Forgetting an ex after a long relationship involves grief. Forgetting a crush is more about releasing hope. Forgetting someone who treated you badly can involve rebuilding your self-esteem.

Create real distance

1. Go no contact (or as close as you can)

Every text, like or “just checking in” call reopens the wound. Mute or unfollow him on social media, archive the chat and stop initiating contact. If you share kids, a workplace or a friend group, keep conversations brief, polite and practical.

2. Remove the triggers from your space

Out of sight really does help. Box up gifts, photos and his hoodie. You do not have to throw them away; just put them somewhere you will not see them every day. Change your phone wallpaper if it is a photo of him, and consider a new playlist without “your” songs.

3. Stop checking up on him

Looking at his profile feels like getting information, but it mostly gives your brain another hit of longing. If the urge is strong, delete the app for a week or ask a friend to change your password temporarily.

Tip: When you feel the pull to check his profile or text him, set a 20-minute timer and do something physical — a walk, a shower, dishes. Urges peak and pass more quickly than they feel like they will.

Process what happened

4. Remember the whole story, not the highlight reel

Missing someone tends to edit out the hard parts. Make an honest list of the things that did not work: the times he cancelled, the arguments that never got resolved, the qualities that hurt you. This is not about hating him. It is about seeing the relationship clearly.

5. Treat it as a learning experience

Ask yourself what you learned about what you need, what you will not accept again and how you want to show up in your next relationship. Lessons turn pain into something useful.

6. Let yourself feel it

Pretending you are fine usually makes the process longer. Cry if you need to, journal, talk it out. Feelings that are acknowledged tend to move through; feelings that are pushed down tend to come back at inconvenient moments.

7. Be patient with the timeline

There is no deadline for getting over someone. Some days you will feel great, then a song will knock you sideways. That is normal. Healing is not a straight line, but if you compare this month to last month, you should see progress.

Fill your life back up

8. Get busy with things that are yours

Pick up a hobby you set aside, sign up for a class, train for a 5K, redecorate your room or throw yourself into a work project. Positive distraction is not avoidance; it reminds you that your life is full beyond him. Our list of things to do to move on from a breakup has plenty of ideas.

9. Lean on your people

Friends and family are your best medicine. Tell a couple of trusted people what you are going through and let them check on you. Make plans so your weekends are not empty. If loneliness is hitting hard, read our guide on how to deal with loneliness.

10. Take care of your body

Sleep, food, movement and sunlight sound basic, but heartbreak drains your energy. Small routines, like a morning walk or cooking a real dinner, help you feel steady again.

11. Plan something to look forward to

A weekend trip with friends, a concert, a solo day in a new city: having something on the calendar gives your brain a new focus. New places also create new memories that do not involve him.

12. Date again when you're genuinely ready

Going on a date can be a helpful reminder that there are other interesting people out there. The key word is ready. If you are dating mainly to make him jealous or to numb the hurt, wait a little longer. When you can enjoy meeting someone new without comparing them to him, you are probably there.

Forgetting a crush vs. forgetting an ex

Not every guy you need to forget was your boyfriend. Letting go of a crush or a situationship comes with its own challenges:

  • There may be no clear ending. Without a breakup conversation, hope lingers. Give yourself the ending: decide, for yourself, that this chapter is closed.
  • You may grieve what could have been. It is okay to feel sad about a relationship that only existed in possibility. The feelings are still real.
  • Mixed signals keep you hooked. If he texts just often enough to keep you interested but never commits, that inconsistency is your answer. Someone who wants you makes it clear.

Forgetting an ex after a long relationship often involves more practical untangling: shared friends, belongings, routines and maybe even a home. Be patient with that process. You are not just losing a person; you are rebuilding daily life. Either way, the steps above still apply: create distance, see the situation honestly and invest in a life that feels like yours. Our guide on how to forget someone offers more ideas for both situations.

What if you see him everywhere?

Sometimes total distance is not possible. If he works with you, is in your friend group or co-parents with you:

  • Keep interactions short and neutral. Friendly but brief; save personal updates for your friends.
  • Plan your exits. At group events, arrive with a friend and know when you will leave.
  • Set boundaries with mutual friends. It is okay to say, “I'd rather not hear updates about him for now.”
  • Don't relitigate the relationship. Late-night “closure” conversations rarely provide closure.

Signs you're actually moving on

  • You go hours, then days, without thinking about him.
  • His name no longer gives you a jolt.
  • You can remember good times without wanting to go back.
  • You are excited about plans that have nothing to do with him.
  • You feel curious, not anxious, about meeting someone new.

If weeks become months and you are still stuck, struggling to sleep, eat or function, consider talking to a licensed therapist. Sometimes a breakup stirs up older pain, and support can make a real difference. You can also read how to get over a broken heart and how to stop thinking about your ex for more strategies.

The bottom line

Forgetting a guy happens gradually, through distance, honesty about what went wrong and a life that grows big enough to crowd out the ache. Be kind to yourself in the process. One day soon you will realize you have not thought about him in a while, and that you are genuinely happy. Our guide on how to be happy with yourself is a good next read.
takeaways: Get clear on why you need to let him go and keep that reason handy for weak moments.
No contact, removing reminders and not checking his profile speed up healing.
Let yourself feel the loss, then fill your time with hobbies, friends and plans.
Date again when you can enjoy someone new without comparing them to him.

faq.q: How long does it take to forget a guy?
faq.a: It varies widely depending on how long you were together, how it ended and the support you have. Many people feel noticeably better within a few weeks to a few months. Progress is not linear, so compare how you feel month to month rather than day to day.

faq.q: How do I stop loving a guy who doesn't love me?
faq.a: Accept the reality of his choice, limit contact and stop feeding hope by checking his profile or reading into old messages. Redirect attention to friends, goals and self-care. Feelings fade when they are no longer fed, especially as you build a life that feels full without him.

faq.q: Should I stay friends with a guy I'm trying to forget?
faq.a: Usually not right away. Friendship tends to keep hope and longing alive. Take a period of real distance first. If, months later, you can see him without hurting or hoping, a friendship may be possible, but it is fine if it never happens.

faq.q: Is it normal to still think about him months later?
faq.a: Yes. Memories can resurface for a long time, especially around anniversaries, songs or places you shared. What matters is whether those thoughts are getting less frequent and less painful. If they are not, or you are struggling to function, talking to a therapist can help.
